posts.excerpt: How a single campaign became a two-season monthly content retainer: 20+ shoots for Muskoka Sauna Co., an audience of 70,000 followers, and content built to sell.
posts.seo_title: Content Retainer Case Study: Muskoka Sauna Co.
posts.meta_description: How a monthly content retainer delivered 20+ shoots over two seasons for Muskoka Sauna Co. and grew the brand to 70,000 followers.
posts.author: Coastline Films
posts.body_part_1:
Most premium brands do not have a content problem. They have a consistency problem. They book one big shoot, post the best of it for six weeks, and then the feed goes quiet until someone panics and books the next one. Every gap costs them reach, and every restart costs them momentum they already paid for once.

Muskoka Sauna Co. went the other way. Over two seasons on a monthly content retainer with Coastline Films, we produced more than 20 individual shoots for the brand. The audience grew to 70,000 followers, and the content was built to do one job above everything else: move product. This is the breakdown of how that partnership works, why it works, and what any Ontario brand can take from it.
posts.body_part_2:
The project at a glance

  • Client: The Muskoka Sauna Co.
  • Engagement: Ongoing monthly content retainer
  • Timeline: Two seasons and counting
  • Output: 20+ individual shoots covering cinematic product, lifestyle and brand content
  • Where it runs: Social media, digital advertising and ongoing brand marketing
  • Audience: Grown to 70,000 followers
  • Location: Muskoka, Ontario

You can watch the work on the Muskoka Sauna Co. project page.

The problem with hiring a video crew one shoot at a time

Here is the pattern we see with most consumer brands in Muskoka, Toronto and across Ontario. A launch is coming, so they hire a crew. The crew shows up, shoots a great day, delivers a hero video and a folder of stills, and leaves. The brand has no say in what the next shoot looks like because there is no next shoot yet. Six weeks later, the content is used up.

That model has three hidden costs.

  • You pay the learning curve every time. A new crew has to learn your product, your customer and your look before they can shoot anything useful. That learning is billed to you, every single booking.
  • Your feed goes dark between bookings. Algorithms reward cadence. When you go quiet for a month, you are not standing still. You are falling behind the brands that kept posting.
  • Your ads run on stale creative. Paid social burns through creative fast. If the same three videos have been running since spring, your cost per sale climbs and nobody can tell you why.

None of this shows up on an invoice. It shows up as slower growth, softer sales and a marketing calendar that is always reacting instead of planning.

From one campaign to a full creative partnership

Muskoka Sauna Co. did not start as a retainer. It started as a single campaign. What changed was what happened after: instead of treating that campaign as a finished job, the relationship turned into a long-term creative growth program, with Coastline Films embedded in how the brand is built rather than hired shoot to shoot.

That shift matters more than any piece of gear or any single video. When the same crew shoots a brand month after month, three things happen.

  • The brief gets shorter and the work gets better. We already know the product, the customer and the look. Shoot days go to new ideas, not to re-learning the basics.
  • Every shoot builds on the last one. We can see what landed on social and in ads, and plan the next shoot around it instead of guessing.
  • The brand looks like one brand. Consistent colour, framing and tone across 20+ shoots is what makes a feed feel premium. That is very hard to fake with a rotating cast of freelancers.

What we shoot for Muskoka Sauna Co.

The retainer covers three kinds of content, each with its own job.

Cinematic product content

A sauna is a considered purchase. Nobody buys one on impulse. Product content has to show the build, the materials and the details up close so a buyer feels confident before they ever see one in person. This is the content that answers objections before they are raised, and it is the kind of content that does the heavy lifting in paid ads.

Lifestyle content

Product shots tell people what it is. Lifestyle content tells them what owning one feels like. In Muskoka, the setting does a lot of that work for you. Lifestyle is what stops the scroll and makes someone save the post for later. It is also what turns followers into future customers.

Brand content

Brand content is the layer that holds everything together. It is the work that tells people who Muskoka Sauna Co. is, not only what it sells, and it gives the brand a voice that carries across every channel.

Why shooting across seasons is the real advantage

This is the part one-off shoots cannot copy. A brand like Muskoka Sauna Co. has a different customer mood in every season, and the content has to meet them where they are.

Over two seasons, the retainer let us plan around that instead of trying to cram a year of content into one weekend. The work is shot across seasons and tailored to the customer at every step, from the person who just found the brand to the person who is one ad away from buying. The result is a steady cadence of new material that keeps the brand active and top of mind year-round, not only when there is a launch.

If you shoot a whole year of content in August, it looks like August all year. Your customer notices, even if they could not tell you why.
posts.body_part_3:
The results: 70,000 followers and content that sells

Followers are the number people ask about first, so here it is: Muskoka Sauna Co.'s audience has grown to 70,000 followers over the course of the partnership. That is a real audience for a premium product in a niche category, and it gives the brand a channel it owns for every launch, promotion and season that follows.

But followers were never the goal on their own. The content is designed to grow the audience and consistently move product. Every shoot is planned with a use in mind: an ad, a launch post, a product page, a seasonal push. Nothing is shot just to fill a hard drive.

[JACOB: add a sales result or client quote from Muskoka Sauna Co. here, for example a change in online sales, ad performance or inbound inquiries since the retainer started]

What a monthly content retainer actually looks like

If you have only ever hired a crew for a single day, a retainer can sound like a big commitment. In practice it is simpler than a one-off shoot, because the planning never starts from zero.

  • A planned shoot every month. Dates are on the calendar ahead of time, built around your launches, promotions and seasons.
  • One crew that knows your brand. The same people behind the camera every time, so the look stays consistent and the briefs stay short.
  • Video and photo for every channel. Vertical edits for social, cut-downs for ads, and stills for your site, email and print.
  • A steady flow of fresh creative. Your feed and your ad account never run dry, so you are not scrambling for content the week before a sale.

You can see the full details and pricing on our monthly content retainer page. If you want to compare it against a one-off production, our guide to what video production costs in Ontario breaks down both options in CAD, and the video production cost calculator will give you a realistic range in under a minute.

Is a content retainer right for your brand?

A retainer is not for everyone. It works best when a few things are true.

  • You sell something people need to see before they buy. Premium consumer products, resorts, boats, custom homes. The more considered the purchase, the more content it takes to earn the sale.
  • You already run, or plan to run, paid social. Ads eat creative. A retainer is the cheapest way to keep feeding them.
  • Your business changes with the seasons. If your customer behaves differently in July than in January, your content should too.
  • You want a partner, not a vendor. The value compounds when the same team learns your brand over months, not hours.

If you only need one great piece, such as a brand film you will run for years or a single broadcast spot, a one-off video production is the better buy. We will tell you that on the first call.

What other Ontario brands can take from this

The lesson from Muskoka Sauna Co. is not about saunas. It is about cadence. The brands that win attention in Muskoka, Toronto and across Ontario are rarely the ones with the single biggest shoot. They are the ones that show up every month with something new, look the same every time they show up, and plan every piece of content around a sale.

You can do that with a rotating cast of freelancers and a lot of project management. Or you can hand it to one team that already knows how to do it. See more of our work on the work page, or read about how we cover Muskoka and Toronto video production.

FAQ

What is a monthly content retainer?

It is an ongoing agreement where a production company shoots for your brand every month on a set schedule, delivering video and photo for social, ads and marketing. You get a consistent flow of content from one team instead of booking and briefing a new crew each time.

How many shoots did Coastline Films do for Muskoka Sauna Co.?

More than 20 individual shoots across two seasons, covering cinematic product, lifestyle and brand content.

Is a retainer better than a one-off video shoot?

For brands that post often, run ads or change with the seasons, usually yes. A one-off shoot is better when you need a single hero piece, like a brand film or a broadcast commercial, that you will use for years.

Does Coastline Films work outside Muskoka?

Yes. We work across Muskoka, Toronto and the rest of Ontario, and in British Columbia.

How do I start?

Book a 15-minute call. We will ask about your product, your customer and your calendar, and tell you honestly whether a retainer or a one-off shoot makes more sense.

Want content that keeps your brand moving all year?

If your feed goes quiet between shoots, or your ads are running on creative from last season, that gap is costing you sales right now. Book a 15-minute call and we will map out what a year of content could look like for your brand, season by season.

posts.body_part_1:
TEAMLTD stands for Living The Dream. For almost eight years, that was more or less Jacob DeGrace's job description.

The job was content. The office was wherever the brand was having its best week: a lake in Muskoka, a sand dune in the California desert, an RV parked at a country festival, an ice track in Finland, a raft on the River Kwai. Somebody had to film it. That somebody was Jacob, now the founder of Coastline Films.
posts.body_part_2:
One shoot

If you don't know the brand: TEAMLTD is a Canadian lifestyle apparel company out of Mississauga, founded by two Canadian athletes, Jamie Visser and Scott Croxall, and built around action sports, travel and a good time.

What started as a single video project turned into a full-time job. In 2016, TEAMLTD hired a 17-year-old Jacob to shoot one campaign in Toronto. The video landed, and they offered him a permanent spot on the team.

Summers on the lake

In summer the brand lived in Muskoka, and the calendar ran on parties. There were three big ones, Balapalooza, Sunday Funday and the Giddy Up Country Party, with Monday resort nights filling the gaps between them.

Sunday Funday opened every season at the KEE to Bala on May long weekend: DJs, TEAMLTD giveaways, lights up at 2 a.m. By 2019 it was in its sixth year. The Giddy Up Country Party took Canada Day, and the 2019 edition, its fifth, put Jade Eagleson on stage.

The KEE is also where TEAMLTD hosted the NELK Boys for a weekend. There was beer pong. There was a lot of beer pong.

Winters chasing summer

A summer collection doesn't shoot well in an Ontario January. So after high school, winters meant a flight to California and a base in Huntington Beach, shooting TEAMLTD's Summer Launch campaigns with local models and influencers who could be on set the same afternoon.

Plans were loose and shoots came together fast. Some days it was a rented Chevy Suburban packed with models and blow-up inflatables, pointed at the Glamis sand dunes. Other days it was a rented Jeep Wrangler and the hills above Santa Barbara.

Some nights ended in the Hollywood Hills with the NELK Boys, at parties full of some of the biggest names on the internet. Same beer pong as the KEE. Different zip code.

The Dream Machine

In summer 2018, TEAMLTD and Coors Light put four people in an RV and pointed it at eight Canadian music festivals. The RV was called the Dream Machine. Co-founder Scott Croxall drove. Jacob, Nano Stasiak and Justin Reynolds rode along, with co-founder Jamie Visser and Kris Howes jumping in for stretches. Jacob ran camera.

It started in Timmins at Stars & Thunder: eight days, Arkells, Bryan Adams, Our Lady Peace. Then east to Cavendish Beach in PEI. Then a hungover Monday-morning drive to Quebec City to make the Foo Fighters at Festival d'été. Then Osheaga in Montreal. Then Boots & Hearts in Oro-Medonte.

Boots, as TEAMLTD's recap tells it, went like this. Roll through the gates the minute they open on Wednesday. Claim a spot for the RV. Head back to the office for two days to earn the weekend. Then a surprise morning set from James Barker Band on the Chevy Silverado Pop Up Stage, The Reklaws, Jade Eagleson with Nano shooting, and Thomas Rhett closing it out on Sunday night.

The partnership outlived the summer. In 2019, TEAMLTD was back at Osheaga with Coors Light.
posts.body_part_3:
A gator off the bow

In February 2018, TEAMLTD signed Nic Rapa, an Australian pro wakeboarder ranked second in the world at the time, who split his year between Florida and Australia. He has since piled up six world titles and five Pro Wakeboard Tour championships, and he still rides for TEAMLTD.

When the Nic Rapa x TEAMLTD collection was ready to launch, Jacob, Nano and Kris Howes loaded the truck and drove to Florida to shoot it. Days were BBQ and wakeboarding. Nights were on the water.

One night they went out with Reed Hansen, a wakeskater with eleven world titles who grew up on Central Florida's lakes, to film some catch-and-release. Dark lake, wake boat, one spotlight. They worked the shallow, swampy edges until the beam caught a pair of eyes, then eased the boat into the shallows.

Reed was on the bow. Then he wasn't. He jumped, landed on a three-foot juvenile alligator and came up holding it with his bare hands. He brought it aboard so everyone could meet it, then gave it back to the lake.

Jacob has filmed a lot of things since. That one stays with him.

Crashed Ice and cold water

A big collaboration with Huawei took the team to Europe to put the company's new phones through Finland, Amsterdam and Lisbon. Finland came first, and it came cold.

The trip started in Jyväskylä at Red Bull Crashed Ice, where Scott Croxall was racing. Ice cross downhill is four skaters, full contact, down a twisting ice track at up to 80 km/h, and Jyväskylä runs it on natural ice, ruts and all. Scott is more than a guy with a clothing brand: he won the sport's world championship in 2015.

After the race the crew drove deeper into Finland's interior to go dog sledding. One night they had dinner with the whole Red Bull Crashed Ice team, then did it the Finnish way: sauna, then straight into the water through the ice.

Then Amsterdam. Then Lisbon. New phones in hand the whole way.

Two weeks in Thailand

In fall 2019, Contiki Canada and the Tourism Authority of Thailand hosted Jacob and Phil Paquette, better known as Paqs, for two weeks across Thailand. Paqs and his brother Nick won season 4 of Big Brother Canada in 2016, the first siblings to win a Big Brother title anywhere in the world. Jacob wrote the trip up himself in a three-part series on TEAMLTD's blog: Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3.

It started with a run for extra hard drives and a ride to Pearson from Croxy. Twenty-four hours, one Taipei layover and one towel-less airport shower later (they dried off under the blow dryers), they were in Bangkok. Day one was a two-hour traditional Thai massage at a school for the blind, then Chinatown, until a thunderstorm shut the night down.

Then south. A flight to Trang. Deep-fried jackfruit from a roadside stop. A basket-weaving lesson in the jungle. Three hours of road to the wetlands of Phatthalung and a night in huts on stilts, where two room keys meant one good view. Jacob won the draw and woke up to Thailand's largest lagoon, fishing nets strung across the horizon on wooden frames. Local fishermen showed them the lagoon the next day.

The Contiki half ran the other direction. Chang beers turned into Khao San Road, and Khao San Road turned into scorpions. Then a tuk tuk to a market for roasted bugs and tequila, a night on a floating raft on the River Kwai with no power and no plumbing, and Chiang Mai, feeding and bathing elephants at a sanctuary. Of everything, that was the highlight.

First jump

One morning in California, Jacob and Nano woke up with the same idea: they were going to skydive. Not tandem. Their own parachutes.

They drove to Perris, sat through the eight-hour first jump course for PFF Level 1, the first stage of Progressive Freefall training, and made the first skydive of their lives at sunset. It was Jacob's first jump and nowhere near his last. He still skydives today.

Living it

None of it was nine to five. Behind every festival and every flight were a lot of late nights working. The team lived and breathed the brand, and it showed in everything TEAMLTD put online.

That was the whole point. People didn't follow TEAMLTD for the clothes. They followed for the culture, the one the team created and lived every day, on camera and off. They built something special, and it came across exactly that way.

What it left behind

Jacob runs Coastline Films now, a premium video and photo production company in Canada, and a lot of it traces straight back to TEAMLTD. Show up as part of the team, not a vendor who leaves at five. Go where the story is, whether that's a sand dune in the desert or a Finnish winter. Make the thing that travels, the way that first video did.

"From Finland to the Cross Canada TEAMLTD X Coors Light Summer RV Festival road trip it has been nothing but exceptional and professional working with Coastline! Highly recommend!!"

Scott Croxall, co-founder of TEAMLTD, in a Google review of Coastline Films

Some of it stuck in less practical ways. On a 2021 shoot in the Great Bear Rainforest, he left his Living the Dream toque wrapped around a beam at a hot spring on BC's north coast. It might still be up there.

These are just a few of the stories. Almost eight years at TEAMLTD left plenty more where they came from. That chapter is closed now, but it holds some of the best, craziest and wildest times of Jacob's life, and a good part of who he is today. He's still close with the whole team.

posts.name: Four Months on Parlay Revival: Panama, San Blas and Delos
posts.excerpt: A Panama boatyard, weeks of island hopping in San Blas, and a regatta win over SV Delos. Four months aboard one of YouTube's biggest sailing channels.
posts.seo_title: Parlay Revival: Four Months Aboard | Coastline Films
posts.meta_description: Four months aboard Parlay Revival: a Panama haul-out, island life in San Blas, and a regatta win over SV Delos, with Jacob DeGrace on camera.
posts.author: Coastline Films
posts.body_part_1:
Parlay is a 45-foot catamaran that sank in Tortola after Hurricane Irma. Today it's home to one of the biggest sailing channels on YouTube, and for four months it was home to Coastline Films founder Jacob DeGrace, who joined the crew to film and edit the show.

This is the story of those four months: a boatyard in Panama, a few hundred islands off its coast, and a race against another sailing channel.
posts.body_part_2:
What is Parlay Revival?

Parlay Revival is a sailing channel run by Colin MacRae, a New Zealand superyacht engineer some people know from Bravo's reality TV show Below Deck Sailing Yacht. In 2017, Hurricane Irma wrecked a 2012 Lagoon 450 catamaran in Tortola. Colin bought it, rebuilt it with friends, and filmed every step. The rebuild became a channel, and the channel became a way of life: sailing around the world with a rotating crew and putting out a new episode every Sunday.

The channel now sits above 400,000 subscribers and 85 million views. People don't stick around for 400-plus episodes because of drone shots. They stick around because they know the crew and they've been there for every breakdown, fix, and passage.

Life aboard

There's no separate production team on a boat like this. Jacob came aboard as crew first, and the camera came along for all of it. The edit happens wherever there's battery power and a signal, and the Sunday deadline doesn't move.

The haul-out in Panama

Before you cross the Pacific, you take a hard look at your boat. Parlay's turned up bulkhead damage, the structural panels that hold a catamaran together under load. That's not a cosmetic fix, and it's not something you take across thousands of miles of open ocean. The boat came out of the water in Panama and the crossing went on hold.

Boatyard life is nothing like life at anchor. The boat sits on stands, the days run on a repair list, and the weather window for the crossing keeps getting closer. No sailing, no new islands, no fixed date to leave.

For the channel, it's the hardest stretch to film. The yard episodes had to make the waiting worth watching: the stakes, the setbacks, the fixes, and the people grinding through them. Jacob edited some of the most important episodes of that stretch on board, while the work went on around him. When Parlay finally went back in the water, the audience had earned that moment with the crew.

San Blas

With Parlay back in the water, the crew pointed her at San Blas.

The San Blas Islands sit off Panama's Caribbean coast inside Guna Yala, a territory governed by the Guna people. It's a few hundred small islands, most of them sand, palms, and reef, and plenty you can walk around in ten minutes. For weeks that was home. The crew island hopped, dropped anchor wherever looked good, and spent time with the Guna communities on the islands they visited.

Countless nights turned into a dinghy ride to shore, a bonfire, and dinner on the beach with the locals. Then the beers came out, then the dancing around the fire started, and nobody was ever in a hurry to get back to the boat.

New Year's Eve was a fireworks show on a private island, with Parlay and about 15 other sailboats anchored off the beach. Clear sky, no city glow, nothing between the fleet and the show.

San Blas isn't known as a surf trip, but some of the atolls around the islands have reef breaks if you go looking. The crew would run the dinghy out and surf whatever was working.

Reef breaks come with a cost. First wave one morning, Jacob came off and landed his foot square on fire coral. He pulled the chunk out of the bottom of his foot, sat out the session in the dinghy, then headed back to Parlay to soak it in a bucket of the hottest lemon water the galley could make. First wave of the day was also the last.

None of it was a shoot. It was just life on the boat, which is exactly why it worked on camera.

Delos vs. Parlay

San Blas is also where Parlay met up with SV Delos, Brian Trautman's crew and another of YouTube's big sailing channels. Two boats in one anchorage turns into a race fast. This one turned into a full regatta: Delos, a heavy bluewater cruising ketch, against Parlay, a Lagoon 450 production catamaran. Plus beach fires, drinks, and a lot of new friends.

Parlay took it. Afterward, a photo of the winning Parlay crew went up on the wall aboard Delos, which is about as good as a trophy gets between two boats.
posts.body_part_3:
Both channels told the story, and a lot of the aerials came off Jacob's drone. When Delos released their side of it, Brian credited Jacob and Parlay for sharing “all the amazing footage and especially drone shots.”

Two crews, two audiences, one race, and footage that carried both edits.

Looking back

Four months, one boatyard, a few hundred islands, and a regatta win against another of YouTube's big sailing crews. Parlay went on to cross the Pacific, and the channel is still putting out an episode every Sunday. That stretch in Panama is a good reminder of why people watch: not for the boat, but for the people on it, and for everything nobody planned.

See more of our work here.

posts.name: Wrong Lens, Right Bear: Filming the Great Bear Rainforest
posts.excerpt: A week aboard Swell on BC's north coast, filming for Maple Leaf Adventures. Twenty humpbacks, a bear named Big Nick, and the best footage came from the wrong lens.
posts.seo_title: Filming the Great Bear Rainforest | Coastline Films
posts.meta_description: Field notes from a week filming the Great Bear Rainforest aboard Swell for Maple Leaf Adventures: humpbacks, grizzlies and a film with 2M+ views.
posts.author: Coastline Films
posts.og_image_caption: The Swell is a historic 88-foot Canadian tugboat built in 1912 by Arthur Moscrop for the Victoria Tug Company—the very same year the RMS Titanic set sail. Originally operating as a coal-fired steam vessel, it spent 92 years transporting vital cargo like wood and machinery along the rugged coast of British Columbia. Over its near-century as a commercial workboat, it underwent major transformations, including converting to a diesel engine in 1954, serving as a private yacht, and appearing on the classic Canadian TV show The Beachcombers in 1974. Following extensive multi-million dollar refits, this iconic wooden-hulled vessel was beautifully repurposed by Maple Leaf Adventures as a boutique, eco-friendly expedition cruise ship. Today, it accommodates up to 12 guests in private cabins, charting passenger excursions through the remote wilderness, fjords, and wildlife habitats of British Columbia and Alaska's Inside Passage
posts.body_part_1:
In October 2021, Brodie and Jacob spent a week aboard Swell, a classic tugboat Maple Leaf Adventures runs through the Great Bear Rainforest on BC's north coast. The job was to come home with a film that made people want to book the trip. I kept a journal most nights. This is what's in it, cleaned up a bit.

The Great Bear has no roads. You get around by boat, you go ashore by zodiac, and the schedule belongs to the tide and the animals. We had a shot list. The bears did not read it.
posts.body_part_2:
Terrace to Kitimat

We flew into Terrace and had a beer at the airport restaurant, mostly because it was the last wifi we'd see all week and we still had edits to send. Then a cab to the marina in Kitimat, in the rain.

Our cabin was about three feet wide and six feet long, with two bunks. It was all the room we needed. Dinner was three courses in the salon with a boat full of strangers from across Canada and the US, each there for their own reasons, and more than a couple of glasses of wine. We finished the night trading stories.

Whale Channel

Day two started in Eagle Bay with the rain finally letting up. On the way to shore, our zodiac driver took us straight through the stream coming out of Swell's bilge pump, so everyone started the morning with a wet back. The beach was quiet. No wildlife, so after an hour we went back to the boat.

The plan was to run Whale Channel looking for humpbacks. We found the first one before we got there. The captain cut the engine, we drifted to a stop and everyone went up top. Five minutes later it surfaced and exhaled. Then another came up, then another. Over about an hour and a half we counted roughly 20 breaches.

We filmed them surfacing, blowing and diving. At one point I was on a whale that showed its tail and went deep, which usually means a few minutes before you see it again, so I swung over to another group. Thirty seconds later the first one breached, its whole body clear of the water. I didn't get the shot. I watched it instead, which in hindsight was the better use of those few seconds.

We stayed with the whales so long we had to anchor in Home Bay, an hour short of where we'd planned to be. At dinner the conversation turned to pirates. Brodie has met an actual one, or at least a man called Pigeon who sails the waters off Vancouver Island and fits the description. He was mid-story when a light appeared off the starboard side, close enough that the captain got up to check. It was a fishing boat two kilometres away. Hot tub, early night.

The outer coast

The anchor came up at 6:30 the next morning and woke everyone on board except me. I sleep deep. By the time I opened the cabin door we were moving through thick fog and light rain, just before first light.

By 8:45 we were in the zodiacs off a small island covered in seals. Brodie, Simon from the crew and I had a boat to ourselves. Brodie had his underwater housing ready to go. The seals were not interested. On the way back a humpback blew somewhere in the distance, loud enough to turn every head in the boat.

The next stop meant rounding the end of Whale Channel into the almost open Pacific. Swell rolled the whole way and about half the guests got seasick. On the other side were white sand beaches with surf breaking on them, and the landing filled everyone's rubber boots.

Ashore it looked like Jurassic Park. I remember thinking it was the wildest place I'd been without leaving Canada. An hour in, it started pouring, and the tide had come up further than any of us noticed. Simon ran the zodiac around to a better spot and we scrambled in.

Back on Swell, Brodie decided to swan dive off the bow. There were lion's mane jellyfish in the water around the boat. He didn't care. I put the drone up and got the shot.

Heading north toward Gribbell Island, the sky cleared completely. Brodie and I got in the hot tub, which we more or less had to ourselves all week, and watched four bald eagles meet over the water and circle off the stern. My camera was downstairs. Some things you're allowed to just watch.

That evening I watched the sun go down from the back deck, on the couch next to a 77-year-old man. We talked for a long time about life and how it looks from the far end of a full one.

Gribbell Island

We were up before first light for the thirty-minute run to Gribbell Island, where we met Marvin, the local Indigenous guide who'd be with us all day. Marvin grew up on these islands and knows every bear by name. He also turned out to be one of the people featured in the IMAX film Great Bear Rainforest. Gribbell is bear country even by Great Bear standards, and you feel it the second you step off the zodiac.

The hike to the viewing spot climbs through thick rainforest on ground so boggy every step makes its own sound. Then you sit. We knew we'd be there about eight hours. For the first few, nothing happened. Someone opened the food bins, we had cookies and coffee, and we started wondering out loud whether this was going to be one of those days.

Then a big black bear the guides call Big Nick came slowly around the corner. Nobody saw him coming until he was about ten feet from our naturalist. He saw us, turned around and crossed the river to get out of our way, then spent the next half hour fishing salmon out of it, pinning them and taking them apart.

Later we watched two bears fight, which settles any question about who's in charge out there. What stuck with me was the other side of it. An animal that strong will walk within ten feet of a group of people, look you over and go back to eating. You're not a threat. You're just there.

The day's count: three bears, a pine marten, a lot of birds and a long conversation with Marvin. The tide was high by the time we got back to the beach, so we stood on what was left of it and waited for the zodiac.
posts.body_part_3:
Khutze Inlet

In Khutze I woke up to water dripping on my face. Swell's engine had started and shaken the condensation off the skylight above my bunk. It was close to freezing and I was still cold from the day before, so that was a great start. Breakfast fixed it: eggs Benedict with sausage and greens, my favourite of the trip.

The plan was grizzlies in the estuary, all day, in the rain. We spotted the first one five minutes out, digging roots on the shoreline. He was shy and left. There were bald eagles in nearly every tree. We ran aground a few times at low tide and paddled ourselves off. On the north side we found a mother and two cubs in the bushes, and they were gone before anyone got anything usable.

Three hours in, my rain pants had quit and my base layer was soaked. The group headed back to the boat to warm up.

Brodie and I stayed out with Simon to pull the crab traps, mostly for the footage. My hands barely worked the camera. We pulled seven crab, three of them keepers. Then Simon pointed back toward the estuary. Bear. The four of us in the boat looked at each other, cold and wet, and nobody said no.

Khutze had given us three short encounters so far and nothing we could build a film around. This was the last chance before Swell moved on. It was also when Brodie and I realized we only had 16-35mm lenses with us. Those are wide angles. Unless you're about ten feet from a bear, they're the wrong tool.

We eased in. The bear didn't leave. We kept going and he kept not leaving, until we were close enough that the wide lenses were exactly right. For about thirty minutes he ate a salmon and dug for roots while we filmed. We came back with more than we'd hoped for.

Being that close to a grizzly while he eats is hard to explain. You can see his eyes. He isn't the killing machine he gets made out to be. What it felt like, mostly, was mutual respect.

We didn't make a big deal of it at dinner. I got in the hot tub to write and thaw out my hands, and Simon came around the corner to tell us the crab had to go back in. Crab season had closed the day before. We let them go. If we'd known that before we went out, we never would have pulled the traps, and we never would have found that bear.

The hot springs

Day seven was a transit day, four hours on the boat. By then, day one felt like a month ago. Brodie and I spent most of the run in the hot tub with a cold beer. When we anchored, everyone changed for the hot springs. I'd forgotten swim trunks at home, so a pair of underwear got promoted for the week.

It was a short zodiac ride and a short walk in cold rain, everyone in one layer and a rain shell. The springs have two pools, one a little hotter than the other, both around 100°F. Hanging from the roof of the shelter are hundreds of buoys, lures and odds and ends, all signed by people who've soaked there. Some go back to the 1980s.

We stayed about two hours. On the way out I wanted to leave something like everyone else had, but I didn't have a lure or anything nautical. So I wrapped my toque around a ceiling beam with the Living the Dream logo facing out. One day I'd like to go back and see if it's still up there.

The film

Maple Leaf Adventures released the film in April 2022. It has passed 2 million views on their Facebook page alone, and pulled a big audience on YouTube on top of that. For a place most people will never see in person, that's the whole job: get it in front of people and make them want to go.

Photography and video by Jacob DeGrace and Brodie DeGrace of Coastline Films, aboard Swell with Maple Leaf Adventures, October 2021.

If you run trips like this and want people to feel them before they book, it's the work we like most. Tell us about yours.

What Maple Leaf said

It's been a pleasure seeing our wild west coast through the lens of Coastline Films! The team's talent, technical skill and amenability to feedback made working together a breeze. The result is a beautiful piece of storytelling that we can't wait to share with the world.

Jordan Lambe
Marketing Director · Maple Leaf Adventures

posts.author: Coastline Films
posts.body_part_1:
We keep six playlists going. A couple are tight, forty-odd songs we'd defend to anyone. The others have been growing for years and are closing in on a thousand tracks, mostly because nobody wants to be the one who deletes anything.

They're what we put on for long drives, slow mornings and late nights in the edit. All six are public. Here's what's on each one, and when we reach for it.
posts.body_part_2:
Tap a cover to jump to a playlist, or hit play and read along.

Temple Hunting Tunes

94 tracks | "get rad."

The name started literally: old temples at the end of jungle roads, the kind you only find by taking the wrong turn on purpose. It stuck because temple hunting ended up describing most of what we do on our days off. Your temple might be a reef break with nobody on it, a lake at the end of a logging road, or a diner that's been open since 1962. It's whatever place is worth the drive, and the drive is half the point.

The music comes from the same kind of searching. Desert blues out of the Sahara from Tinariwen and Bombino. Zamrock from 1970s Zambia. Ethio-jazz, Nigerian funk, Thai luk thung and Vietnamese sixties pop, with some Peruvian chicha and surf rock mixed in. Most of it was recorded a long way from here, and it sounds like heat, dust and roads that don't show up on the map.

  • Play it when: you're driving toward a pin on the map with no cell service and no real plan.
  • Sounds like: hypnotic guitars, warm horns and a groove that doesn't let up.
  • Liner note: start with "Tamalla" by Vieux Farka Touré and Khruangbin, then let it run.

Listen to Temple Hunting Tunes on Spotify

Tofino Dawg Days

976 tracks | "Louder!"

Named for those long west coast summer stretches: surf in the morning, nowhere to be in the afternoon, and a sunset that refuses to quit. The description says it all. If it's worth playing, it's worth playing loud.

That goes for most things. Half-hearted is boring. Commit to the idea, turn it up and see what happens.

  • Play it when: windows down, wetsuit drying on the dash, nowhere to be until the tide turns.
  • Sounds like: long summer days that never end on time.
  • Liner note: 976 tracks. This isn't a playlist, it's a whole season. Hit shuffle and commit.

Listen to Tofino Dawg Days on Spotify

Mint

987 tracks | "It's pretty mint."

"Mint" is our highest compliment. A clean wave, a perfect cup of coffee, a frame that lands exactly right. Not flashy, not overdone. Just right.

This is the everyday list, the one that's always on in the background. It's the biggest of the six because it's the one we never stop adding to.

  • Play it when: you need to lock in for hours and not think about what's playing.
  • Sounds like: smooth, steady and easy on the ears.
  • Liner note: 987 tracks and counting.

Listen to Mint on Spotify
posts.body_part_3:
Groovin

230 tracks

Some days just flow. Everyone is moving together, nothing needs explaining, and the whole thing feels easy. That's the groove, and it's hard to fake.

Groovin is the list that gets you there. Head-nod tempo, the kind of beat that makes loading the truck or cleaning the kitchen feel like part of the fun.

  • Play it when: loading gear, cooking dinner, Sunday cleanup.
  • Sounds like: head-nod tempo from start to finish.
  • Liner note: 230 tracks and no description, because it doesn't need one.

Listen to Groovin on Spotify

Vintage Moto

65 tracks | "Cheeeyaaaaa"

Say it out loud. Cheeeyaaaaa is pure stoke: the noise you make when the old bike finally fires up, the swell shows up on time, or the plan actually works.

Vintage Moto is old-school, gritty and short on purpose. It sounds like a carburetor that needs tuning and a road that doesn't need a destination.

  • Play it when: open road, old bike, no plan past lunch.
  • Sounds like: warm, gritty and a little sun-faded.
  • Liner note: 65 tracks. No filler, and no excuse to skip.

Listen to Vintage Moto on Spotify

The Soundtrack

42 tracks | "This is the soundtrack"

The description isn't lazy, it's literal. These are the songs that make a regular drive feel like the opening scene of a movie. The ones you end up remembering a whole trip by, years later.

It's also the most cinematic list we have, and more than a few of our edits started right here: hear a song, picture the shot.

  • Play it when: you're dreaming something up, or it's late and you want to feel something.
  • Sounds like: slow-building and cinematic.
  • Liner note: our tightest list at 42 tracks. Every one has earned its spot.

Listen to The Soundtrack on Spotify

Can you use these songs in your own videos?

Short answer: not for a business. Most of these tracks are commercially licensed, so dropping one into an ad or a company post usually gets it muted or taken down. When we make something for a client, the music is licensed properly. If you love a vibe from one of these lists, tell us and we'll find something that hits the same way.

Follow along

All six playlists are public, and we add to them constantly. Follow Coastline Films on Spotify to catch the updates. Got a track that belongs on one of these lists? Send it to us on Instagram. The best ones make the cut.

And if your brand runs on the same energy, let's make something together.

Your best salesperson is a finished home. The problem is that only a handful of people ever walk through it. Everyone else decides whether to call you based on your website and your Instagram, and for most custom builders that means phone photos from site walks and a gallery that has not been updated in years.

Meanwhile, the people building $1.5M to $5M homes in Muskoka, the GTA and the Sea to Sky are scrolling through builders who look premium on screen. They shortlist on what they see before they ever call. If your work looks average online, you get compared on price. If it looks exceptional, you get compared on fit.
posts.body_part_2:
This guide covers what builder videography actually costs in 2026, what to film at each stage of a build, and how to turn one shoot into months of content. All numbers are in CAD.

How much does videography cost for a custom home builder?

For professional work from an established production company, these are realistic 2026 ranges in Ontario:

  • Finished home shoot (video and photo, 1 day): $3,000 to $8,000
  • Full build story (multiple site visits, start to finish): $8,000 to $20,000
  • Brand film about your company: $8,000 to $25,000
  • Monthly content retainer: $1,800 to $5,000 per month

In BC, including Squamish, Whistler and West Vancouver, expect roughly 15 percent more because crew and gear are in higher demand. A real estate listing video is cheaper, usually under $1,500, but it is built to sell one house fast, not to sell your company to your next client. Those are different jobs.

What to film: the shots that win builds

Clients are not buying a house. They are buying confidence that you will build their house right. Your content should prove three things: craftsmanship, process and the finished result.

1. The finished home, shot like a magazine

Golden hour exteriors, drone reveals of the home in its setting, slow interior walkthroughs, and close-ups of the details you are proud of: millwork, stone, steel and joinery. This is the hero content for your website and ads. Shoot it after staging and landscaping are done, or it will look unfinished on screen.

2. The build in progress

Excavation, framing against the sky, the roof going on, trades at work. Process footage is what separates a builder from a listing. It shows the work buyers never see and makes the finished home mean more. Two to four short site visits across a build is enough.

3. Your people

A short interview with the owner, the site lead walking the frame, a trade explaining why you do it the slow way. Builders sell trust, and trust comes from faces. Ten seconds of you on camera does more than a paragraph of copy about quality.

4. Client stories

A homeowner on their dock or in their kitchen, talking about what it was like to build with you. One honest testimonial video will outsell every other piece of content you own. Ask at the handover, when the excitement is highest.

5. Short vertical edits

Every shoot should produce 10 to 20 short clips for Instagram, Facebook and ads: before and after transitions, detail shots, drone reveals and quick walkthroughs. This is where your posting volume comes from.
posts.body_part_3:
One-off shoot or monthly retainer?

A one-off shoot works when you have one standout project to showcase. You get a hero video and a photo set, and you are done.

Most builders need more than that. A custom build runs 12 to 24 months, and the best content comes from following it from dirt to handover. A monthly retainer means we show up at the right moments, capture every stage, and deliver fresh content every month. Your feed stays active between handovers, and every project becomes a case study. Coastline Films retainers start from $1,800 per month CAD.

See how we approached this for Muskoka builder HLD Muskoka.

How builders actually use the content

  • Website: a hero video on your homepage and a film for each featured project.
  • Instagram and Facebook: two to four posts a week from one month of footage.
  • Paid ads: drone reveals and walkthroughs aimed at people buying land or planning a custom home in your area.
  • Sales meetings: send a build story video before the first meeting so prospects arrive already sold on your process.
  • Recruiting: good trades want to work for builders who look like the best in the area.

What to ask before you hire a videographer

Ask to see builder or architecture work specifically, not weddings or events. Ask whether drone is included and whether the pilot holds a Transport Canada advanced certificate for flying near people and buildings. Ask how many edits and photos you get, in what formats, and whether you can use the footage in paid ads. If they cannot answer clearly, keep looking.

Frequently asked questions

How much does a custom home video cost?

A professionally shot finished home video with photos typically costs $3,000 to $8,000 CAD for a single day in Ontario, and about 15 percent more in BC. A full build story filmed across multiple site visits runs $8,000 to $20,000.

When is the best time to film a finished custom home?

After staging, landscaping and final cleaning, ideally from late spring to early fall for green surroundings and long golden hours. In Muskoka and the Sea to Sky, fall colour and fresh snow can also make standout content if the property is ready.

Is drone footage worth it for home builders?

Almost always. A drone shows the home in its setting: the lot, the water and the scale of the build, which is often what sells a premium property. Make sure your videographer holds the right Transport Canada drone certificate.

How often should a builder post video content?

Two to four times a week on Instagram is a strong cadence. One well-planned shoot day a month can cover that.

Do you work outside Muskoka?

Yes. Coastline Films works across Muskoka, the GTA and the rest of Ontario, plus Squamish, Whistler, Vancouver and Vancouver Island in BC. We also regularly travel for work, Canada-wide and beyond.

Get a real number for your next build

Book a 15-minute call. Tell us about your current projects and where you want to be seen, and we will tell you exactly what it would take, whether that is one finished home shoot or a monthly retainer starting from $1,800 per month. Prefer to estimate first? Try the video production cost calculator.

posts.body_part_1:
Most businesses in BC go looking for a video production price the same way: they email three Vancouver companies, get three quotes that are $5,000, $22,000 and $80,000 apart, and have no idea which one is right. So they either pick the cheapest one and get content that does nothing, or they put the whole thing off another quarter.

They are the ones taking the Tofino bookings, the Squamish home contracts and the Sea to Sky adventure sales you should be getting.
posts.body_part_2:
This guide is the conversation we have with almost every new client at Coastline Films. Here is what video production actually costs across Vancouver, Squamish, Tofino and the rest of BC in 2026, what drives the price up or down, and how to tell whether you should be buying a one-off shoot or a monthly content retainer. All numbers are in CAD.

How much does video production cost in Vancouver? The short answer

For professional work from an established production company in Vancouver, Squamish, Tofino or anywhere else in BC, these are realistic 2026 ranges:

  • Social content shoot: $1,750 to $6,000
  • Brand film (60 to 120 seconds): $9,500 to $40,000
  • Multi-asset campaign: $23,000 to $85,000
  • National broadcast commercial: $85,000 to $275,000+
  • Monthly content retainer: $1,800 to $10,000+ per month

Vancouver prices run roughly 15 to 20 percent higher than most of Canada. The reason is simple: BC's film industry is one of the busiest on the continent, which keeps experienced crew booked and gear in demand year-round. That raises the floor on what a serious production day costs.

If a quote lands far below these ranges, someone is cutting a corner: no pre-production, one person doing everything, no colour grade, stock music, or no usage rights spelled out. If it lands far above, you are usually paying for broadcast-level crew, union talent, travel to Tofino or the Interior, or an agency markup on top of the production company.

The range is wide because "a video" is not one product. The rest of this guide breaks down exactly where the money goes.

What actually drives the cost of a video in BC

Every quote is built from the same handful of levers. Once you understand them, you can read any Vancouver proposal and know whether it is fair.

1. Pre-production: the part you do not see

Concept, script or story outline, shot list, location scouting, scheduling, talent casting and permits. On a small social shoot this might be a few hours. On a brand film shooting in Pacific Rim National Park or on First Nations land, pre-production can run two to four weeks because of permitting, consultation and tide windows. Expect pre-production to be roughly 10 to 20 percent of the budget.

This is the line item cheap quotes skip, and it is the one that decides whether the final video actually sells anything. A shoot without a plan is just expensive footage.

2. Shoot days and crew size

This is the biggest single driver, and the one where Vancouver pricing really diverges from the rest of Canada. A lean crew of one or two (director/shooter plus an assistant or drone operator) for a day typically runs $3,000 to $7,000. Add a dedicated director of photography, gaffer, sound, producer and hair and makeup, and a single day can move to $12,000 to $30,000 before talent and locations.

The trick is matching crew size to what the content actually needs. A lifestyle shoot for a Squamish gear brand's Instagram does not need a 15-person crew. A national broadcast spot does.

3. Gear: cinema cameras, lenses, drones, lighting and weather protection

Cinema camera packages, quality lenses, drones, gimbals and lighting are usually built into a day rate or listed separately. On the BC coast, in the rainforest or in the alpine, add specialty gear: proper rain covers, extra batteries for cold shoots, dry bags, boat mounts for Howe Sound and the Broken Group Islands, and splash housings for surf and water work. This is where premium work separates itself visually, especially in weather that would stop a lighter kit cold.

4. Locations, travel and logistics

Shooting at your own lodge, showroom or job site is the cheapest option. Renting a studio in East Van, a cottage on Bowen Island, or a boat in Clayoquot Sound adds cost. So does travel: a Vancouver crew driving the Sea to Sky to Squamish or Whistler, flying to Tofino via Pacific Coastal, or ferrying gear to Vancouver Island means mileage, accommodation and per diems.

Being based in Squamish with reach into Vancouver, the Sea to Sky corridor and Vancouver Island means we can cover most BC coastal work without the travel line blowing up the budget.

5. Talent

Using your own staff, guides or customers is free, and often more authentic for outdoor and hospitality brands. Professional actors and models cost from a few hundred dollars per day for non-union lifestyle talent to significantly more for ACTRA union performers on a broadcast spot. BC's union presence is strong because of the film industry, so if your project is national or broadcast, expect union rates and buyout fees based on where and how long the ad runs.

6. Post-production

Editing, colour grading, sound design and mixing, licensed music, motion graphics and revisions. A good rule: post-production takes as long as, or longer than, the shoot. Cutting one hero video plus ten short social cuts in vertical and horizontal formats is real work, and it should be priced like it.

7. Usage rights and deliverables

How many versions do you need, in what formats, and where will they run? Organic social is the simplest. Paid ads, TV broadcast and out-of-home add music licensing and talent usage costs. Always make sure your quote spells out what you own and where you can use it.

Sample budgets: what different BC businesses typically spend

Here is how those levers come together for the kinds of businesses we work with across the coast.

A Tofino lodge or Sea to Sky resort launching a new season

Two shoot days on property, a lean-to-mid crew, drone, lifestyle talent, one 60 to 90 second hero film and 10 to 15 short social cuts. Typical range: $15,000 to $35,000. Our work with Black Rock Resort in Ucluelet is an example of this kind of cinematic, booking-focused content on the BC coast.

A Squamish, Whistler or West Vancouver custom home builder

One to two days capturing completed homes in their setting, plus process footage on active sites. Clean, design-driven cinematography and photography cut for Instagram and ads. Typical range: $6,000 to $18,000 per campaign. See how we approached this for Muskoka builder HLD, which is the same system we bring to Sea to Sky builders.

A Pacific coast marine, surf or outdoor brand

Product and lifestyle shooting, often on the water or in the alpine, with drone and detail shots across multiple products or activities. Typical range: $12,000 to $45,000 depending on the number of products and locations. Our Pride Marina campaign is a good reference point for how we build out marine content.

A national brand running a broadcast campaign

Full crew, casting, multiple locations across the country, a hero broadcast spot and months of social rollout. Typical range: $75,000 and up. The Rentals.ca "Find Your Space" campaign shows what that scale of production looks like.
posts.body_part_3:
One-off shoot vs monthly retainer: which one is cheaper?

This is the question that matters most, and the answer surprises people.

A one-off shoot is the right call when you have a single, clear moment: a lodge opening in Tofino, a new Squamish home development reveal, a broadcast campaign, a brand film you will use for years. You pay once, you get a polished asset, and you are done.

The problem is that most businesses do not have a "one video" problem. They have a "we need to show up every week and we have nothing to post" problem. One-off shoots solve that for about six weeks. Then the content runs dry, the feed goes quiet, and you are back to quoting another shoot from scratch. Every time you restart, you pay again for pre-production, onboarding and a crew that has to learn your brand all over again.

A monthly content retainer flips that. You get a set number of shoot days and deliverables every month, the same team every time, and a production partner that already knows your product, your customer and your look. Pre-production gets faster, every shoot builds on the last one, and the cost per finished piece of content drops hard.

At Coastline Films, retainers start from $1,800 per month CAD. That is less than many Vancouver companies charge for a single shoot day, spread into a consistent content engine instead of a one-time spike.

What a retainer looks like in practice

Our longest-running example is Muskoka Sauna Co. What started as a single campaign turned into an ongoing monthly retainer: more than 20 individual shoots across two seasons, covering cinematic product, lifestyle and brand content. Over that time the brand built an audience of 70,000 followers, with a steady cadence of new content that keeps them top of mind year-round and keeps product moving.

That result does not come from one great video. It comes from showing up with great content every single month. It is the same system we are bringing to BC clients from our new Squamish base.

How to get an accurate video production quote in BC

The tighter you can describe what you need, the tighter the quote. Walk in with answers to these: who are you selling to, where will the content run, how many finished pieces do you need, do you have talent and locations or do we source them, and what is the deadline. Any production company that cannot sharpen those with you in a 15-minute call is not the right partner.

Red flags when comparing Vancouver quotes

Watch out for a quote with no breakdown of pre-production, shoot and post, a day rate without a crew list, no mention of colour grade or sound mix, no licensed music budget, vague deliverables ("a few social videos"), and no usage rights spelled out. If you cannot see where the money goes, you cannot judge whether it is fair.

The fastest way to judge a production company is to watch their work. Browse our portfolio and ask yourself one question: does this look like the brand you want to be?

Frequently asked questions

How much does a 1 minute video cost in Vancouver?

A professionally produced 60 second video typically costs $3,500 to $18,000 CAD in BC. A simple social piece with a lean crew sits at the low end. A scripted brand video with talent, multiple locations and a full colour grade and sound mix sits at the high end. Length matters far less than shoot days, crew and post-production.

What is the day rate for a videographer in Vancouver, Squamish or Tofino?

A solo professional videographer typically charges $1,200 to $3,000 per day in BC. A small production crew with a director, camera operator and gear package usually runs $3,000 to $7,000 per day. Editing is generally billed separately. Rates run slightly higher than most of Canada because BC's film industry keeps crew in constant demand.

Is a monthly video retainer worth it for a small business?

If you post on social or run ads, usually yes. A retainer lowers your cost per piece of content, removes the restart cost of new shoots, and gives you a consistent presence that one-off shoots cannot. Coastline Films retainers start from $1,800 per month CAD.

How long does a video production take?

A simple social shoot can be turned around in one to two weeks. A brand film usually takes four to eight weeks from kickoff to final delivery. Broadcast campaigns can take two to four months including pre-production, casting and revisions. Tofino and remote coastal shoots often add a week for travel windows and weather contingency.

Do you travel outside Squamish and Vancouver?

Yes. Coastline Films is based in Squamish with regular work across Metro Vancouver, the Sea to Sky corridor, Vancouver Island including Tofino and Ucluelet, and the BC Interior. We also regularly travel for work, Canada-wide and beyond.

Get a real number for your project

Every business is different, and the right budget depends on what you are trying to sell. The fastest way to get a clear, honest number is a quick conversation.

Book a 15-minute call with Coastline Films. Tell us what you are trying to achieve, and we will tell you exactly what it would take, whether that is a single shoot in Vancouver, Squamish or Tofino, a monthly retainer starting from $1,800 per month, or both. No pressure, no fluff, just a straight answer.

Book your 15-minute call here.
